title: Dear Fellow Shareholders, 2025 was a transformational year for Velo3D, one in which we demonstrated that our technology, our team, and our strategy are aligned to capture a generational opportunity in advanced manufacturing. For the full year, we delivered revenue of $46 million, representing 12% growth over the prior year, and 28% growth when excluding a one-time licensing item in 2024. This progress was driven by expanding demand for our Rapid Production Solutions (RPS) and growing adoption of our large-format Sapphire XC systems across defense and aerospace programs. We exited the year with a record backlog of $31 million, nearly double the $16 million at the close of 2024, built on the strongest quarterly bookings in our company's history. This backlog is expected to convert within the next twelve months and reflects the accelerating shift from prototyping to sustained, full-rate production among our customers. In 2025, we achieved several milestones that we believe fundamentally strengthen our competitive position. We became the first additive manufacturing vendor qualified under the U.S. Army's Ground Vehicle Systems Center initiative and entered into a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with DEVCOM to advance AM solutions for critical defense supply chain challenges. We secured a $32.6 million contract supporting Project FORGE, aimed at eliminating bottlenecks in defense component production. We also won a multiyear, $11.5 million full-rate production contract with a major defense prime contractor, a clear signal that our technology has moved beyond development and into mission-critical, volume manufacturing. On the commercial side, our partnership with Intergalactic, a GE Aerospace company, demonstrated the speed and precision of our platform by going from design to printed IN718 microtube heat exchanger headers in a matter of weeks. These wins underscore a central theme: Velo3D's technology is becoming essential infrastructure for customers who require speed, quality, and resilience in their supply chains. We substantially strengthened our balance sheet during the year, ending 2025 with $39 million in cash, compared to $1.2 million at the close of 2024. In early 2026, we further deleveraged by converting $15 million of debt into equity, reducing outstanding debt by approximately 60% and positioning the company on a much stronger financial footing. Looking ahead, the demand signals are clear. Programs that begin with a single system are expanding to multiple systems, sometimes within months, creating a compounding growth dynamic. Based on the contracts we have secured and the trajectory we are seeing across our customer base, we have developed a long-term capacity plan envisioning up to approximately 400 production systems over the next decade. Our near-term Phase 1 expansion will add capacity for approximately 100 systems at a facility near our California headquarters, optimizing operational efficiency while we build the teams and infrastructure needed for future phases. We are also evaluating selective strategic acquisitions, particularly in feedstock and metal powder, where vertical integration can drive meaningful cost advantages and supply chain resilience as we scale. For 2026, we expect revenue in the range of $60 million to $70 million, with product gross margins projected to exceed 30% in the second half of the year. We expect to achieve EBITDA positive performance in the second half of 2026, a critical inflection point for the company. Beyond the near term, we see Velo3D evolving into something larger than a hardware company. Every build, every part, and every material input across our growing fleet generates high-value manufacturing data. Over time, we intend to build a connected digital manufacturing platform capable of delivering real-time insights across materials science, design optimization, and process performance, creating an additional, durable revenue stream on top of our production business. Velo3D is positioned at the intersection of two powerful forces: the reindustrialization of critical supply chains and the rapid adoption of additive manufacturing at production scale. We intend to be at the forefront of this transformation. Thank you for your continued confidence and support. Sincerely, Arun Jeldi Chairman & Chief Executive Officer Velo3D, Inc.

Young, Anderson Monken, Flora Haberkorn, Eva Van Leemput December 2021 ### Abstract In this note, we first document to what extent companies are facing these supply bottlenecks and which sectors have been affected in a novel way. Specifically, we use textual analysis of earnings calls from the S&P Global Market Intelligence database, which includes 5,000-7,500 earnings calls from U.S. and foreign firms per quarter, to construct firm sentiment indexes about the bottlenecks. The benefit of this approach is that we have very timely data to synthesize information about what firms are seeing on the ground and what challenges they face. Additionally, we can differentiate firm sentiment across different industries. snippet: The Invisible Industrial Base | CNAS ## Introduction When you think about the defense industrial base (DIB), the companies that come to mind are likely ones such as Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin, Huntington Ingalls Industries, General Dynamics, or BAE. If you’re a defense tech denizen, you might think first of Anduril, Saronic, Mach Industries, Northwood, or Castelion. These companies are different by almost every measure: age, number of employees, market cap, annual recurring revenue, operating profit, government revenue, number of locations, political contributions, and lobbying expenditures, to name just a few. Despite those and many more differences, these companies share two important characteristics. First, they are all tier one prime contractors that sell finished products that soldiers, sailors, airmen, marines, and guardians use, shoot, fly, and drive. Second, none of them are 100 percent vertically integrated. In other words, they all rely to some degree on systems, subsystems, components, and subcomponents made by thousands of other companies in tiers two, three, four, five, etc., that most Americans have never heard of but that comprise the foundation of the DIB. Young, Anderson Monken, Flora Haberkorn, Eva Van Leemput December 2021 ### Abstract In this note, we first document to what extent companies are facing these supply bottlenecks and which sectors have been affected in a novel way. Specifically, we use textual analysis of earnings calls from the S&P Global Market Intelligence database, which includes 5,000-7,500 earnings calls from U.S. and foreign firms per quarter, to construct firm sentiment indexes about the bottlenecks. Additionally, we can differentiate firm sentiment across different industries. snippet: The Invisible Industrial Base | CNAS ## Introduction When you think about the defense industrial base (DIB), the companies that come to mind are likely ones such as Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin, Huntington Ingalls Industries, General Dynamics, or BAE. If you’re a defense tech denizen, you might think first of Anduril, Saronic, Mach Industries, Northwood, or Castelion. These companies are different by almost every measure: age, number of employees, market cap, annual recurring revenue, operating profit, government revenue, number of locations, political contributions, and lobbying expenditures, to name just a few. Despite those and many more differences, these companies share two important characteristics. First, they are all tier one prime contractors that sell finished products that soldiers, sailors, airmen, marines, and guardians use, shoot, fly, and drive. Second, none of them are 100 percent vertically integrated. In other words, they all rely to some degree on systems, subsystems, components, and subcomponents made by thousands of other companies in tiers two, three, four, five, etc., that most Americans have never heard of but that comprise the foundation of the DIB. Even with an influx of tens of billions of dollars in private capital into defense and dual-use startups since 2020, the defense industrial base remains shallow and fragile. This is because the lion’s share of this capital has flowed to would-be tier one companies—and subtier suppliers are still reliant on uneven demand signals and appropriations. snippet: The Invisible Industrial Base | CNAS ## Introduction When you think about the defense industrial base (DIB), the companies that come to mind are likely ones such as Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin, Huntington Ingalls Industries, General Dynamics, or BAE. If you’re a defense tech denizen, you might think first of Anduril, Saronic, Mach Industries, Northwood, or Castelion. These companies are different by almost every measure: age, number of employees, market cap, annual recurring revenue, operating profit, government revenue, number of locations, political contributions, and lobbying expenditures, to name just a few. Despite those and many more differences, these companies share two important characteristics. snippet: The Invisible Industrial Base | CNAS ## Introduction When you think about the defense industrial base (DIB), the companies that come to mind are likely ones such as Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin, Huntington Ingalls Industries, General Dynamics, or BAE. If you’re a defense tech denizen, you might think first of Anduril, Saronic, Mach Industries, Northwood, or Castelion. These companies are different by almost every measure: age, number of employees, market cap, annual recurring revenue, operating profit, government revenue, number of locations, political contributions, and lobbying expenditures, to name just a few. Despite those and many more differences, these companies share two important characteristics. First, they are all tier one prime contractors that sell finished products that soldiers, sailors, airmen, marines, and guardians use, shoot, fly, and drive. Second, none of them are 100 percent vertically integrated. In other words, they all rely to some degree on systems, subsystems, components, and subcomponents made by thousands of other companies in tiers two, three, four, five, etc., that most Americans have never heard of but that comprise the foundation of the DIB. Even with an influx of tens of billions of dollars in private capital into defense and dual-use startups since 2020, the defense industrial base remains shallow and fragile. This is because the lion’s share of this capital has flowed to would-be tier one companies—and subtier suppliers are still reliant on uneven demand signals and appropriations. snippet: The Invisible Industrial Base | CNAS ## Introduction When you think about the defense industrial base (DIB), the companies that come to mind are likely ones such as Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin, Huntington Ingalls Industries, General Dynamics, or BAE. If you’re a defense tech denizen, you might think first of Anduril, Saronic, Mach Industries, Northwood, or Castelion. These companies are different by almost every measure: age, number of employees, market cap, annual recurring revenue, operating profit, government revenue, number of locations, political contributions, and lobbying expenditures, to name just a few. Despite those and many more differences, these companies share two important characteristics. First, they are all tier one prime contractors that sell finished products that soldiers, sailors, airmen, marines, and guardians use, shoot, fly, and drive. Second, none of them are 100 percent vertically integrated. In other words, they all rely to some degree on systems, subsystems, components, and subcomponents made by thousands of other companies in tiers two, three, four, five, etc., that most Americans have never heard of but that comprise the foundation of the DIB. Even with an influx of tens of billions of dollars in private capital into defense and dual-use startups since 2020, the defense industrial base remains shallow and fragile. This is because the lion’s share of this capital has flowed to would-be tier one companies—and subtier suppliers are still reliant on uneven demand signals and appropriations.
